title: F1 Teams Bring Major Upgrades to Hungarian GP Ahead of Summer Break
excerpt: Aston Martin unveils Adrian Newey-led B-spec car, Mercedes fixes deployment software bug, and Ferrari adds high-downforce winglets as the Hungaroring hosts the final round before F1's mid-season shutdown.
body:
• Aston Martin introduces a substantially revised AMR26 chassis with significant weight reduction and new aerodynamic surfaces — its first major upgrade after scoring just one point in 10 races
  • Mercedes has identified and patched a software bug in its energy deployment code that cost George Russell straight-line speed at Silverstone and Spa, widening the gap to championship leader Kimi Antonelli to 50 points
  • Ferrari, McLaren, and Red Bull all bring rear wing developments to the high-downforce Hungaroring, with five teams also fielding rookie drivers in Friday's opening practice

Aston Martin's Make-or-Break Moment

Formula 1 arrives at the Hungaroring for round 11 of the 2026 season with a paddock buzzing about upgrade packages — none more significant than the heavily revised Aston Martin AMR26 that Adrian Newey has spent the first half of the season preparing.

https://x.com/Flyin18T/status/2080448982443028674

Aston Martin sit 10th of 11 teams in the constructors' standings with a single point from 10 races. At Spa last weekend, Fernando Alonso finished 19th and last, two laps behind race winner Kimi Antonelli, while Lance Stroll retired with a gearbox failure. Neither driver has progressed beyond Q1 all season.

Rather than follow the conventional pattern of incremental upgrades, Newey made the calculated decision to absorb short-term pain and deliver one sweeping overhaul. The result is a car with a re-homologated and crash-tested forward chassis, substantially revised aerodynamic surfaces, a new nose, modified rear suspension, and significant weight savings that should bring the AMR26 close to the minimum weight limit.

"It was a painful decision. While others have been adding performance, we've effectively been standing still in relative terms, so each weekend can feel more painful than the last. But we believe it's the right decision — the right investment for our future."

— Adrian Newey, Team Principal, Aston Martin

Chief trackside officer Mike Krack confirmed both cars will run the new specification in Hungary. "The reason why we do this is to go racing," Krack told reporters at the Hungaroring on Thursday. "We have not been racing over the last events and this is what we need to return to." A more powerful Honda engine is expected at the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort after the summer break, according to Reuters.

Mercedes Patches the Code That Derailed Russell

Mercedes has made deployment software modifications ahead of Budapest to address the problems that plagued George Russell at Spa-Francorchamps. The team traced the issue to a bug deeply embedded in the calibration code governing energy deployment — a flaw that caused Russell to lose battery power down the Kemmel Straight on the opening lap, leaving him vulnerable to the collision with Lewis Hamilton that ended his race.

A separate software error affected both Mercedes cars at the start of the Belgian GP, reducing energy harvesting at La Source and draining extra battery power through Eau Rouge. The differing ways Russell and Antonelli navigated Eau Rouge meant the consequences were not equal — Russell was locked into a low-power ramp-down mode at 308 km/h, while Antonelli retained enough speed to draft past Max Verstappen.

Russell, now 50 points behind championship leader Antonelli after 10 rounds, described the experience as the "toughest psychological battle" of his career. But he expressed confidence heading to Budapest. "These new power units are just exceptionally complex, and there was something deeply embedded in the calibration of the code that was almost impossible to see unless you knew exactly what to look for," Russell told British media. "I'm glad we have found it."

Team principal Toto Wolff acknowledged it was fortunate the issue was exposed at power-hungry Spa rather than at the energy-rich Hungaroring, where it would have been far harder to detect, according to The Race.

The Rear Wing Arms Race Intensifies

Ferrari has introduced a modified version of its 'Macarena' rear wing featuring a triple-element winglet cascade in the central area — a design borrowing from McLaren's approach at the Monaco Grand Prix. The circuit-specific adaptation is tailored for the Hungaroring's high-downforce demands and is not a precursor to the genuine Macarena 2.0, which Ferrari is developing for its debut at Monza in September, according to RacingNews365.

McLaren, meanwhile, will attempt to get its own flip-over rear wing on track for the first time after an aborted trial at the Austrian Grand Prix. The modified wing will be fitted to Oscar Piastri's MCL40 in first practice alongside a new floor and additional aerodynamic components. McLaren has confirmed the wing will not race before the Italian Grand Prix at the earliest.

Red Bull's technical director Pierre Waché has indicated the team's own Macarena wing — parked at Spa after Max Verstappen's crashes in Austria and Britain were linked to an airflow reattachment problem — has been fixed and could return this weekend.

Drivers as 'Hostages to AI'

The broader story of the Hungarian GP build-up is the growing frustration among drivers with F1's 2026 AI-integrated power units. Energy deployment is governed by self-learning algorithms rather than driver inputs, and the consequences have been stark — qualifying sessions and race results determined by software behaviour rather than driver skill.

"When you've got qualifying decided by computers behaving or misbehaving, it's a pretty crap way of going racing."

— Oscar Piastri, McLaren

Piastri's blunt assessment after Spa echoed complaints from multiple drivers. Some teams have reportedly begun disabling the self-learning algorithms entirely for qualifying sessions to avoid unpredictable deployment, according to The Race. The issue sits at the heart of F1's 2026 regulations, which split power roughly 50-50 between electrical energy and internal combustion.

Five Rookies Get Their Chance

Five teams will field alternate drivers in Friday's opening practice session under mandatory rookie-running regulations. Leonardo Fornaroli returns to the MCL40 for McLaren, replacing Piastri after an impressive fifth-place finish in his FP1 debut at Barcelona. Fred Vesti steps into Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes W17, Paul Aron replaces Franco Colapinto at Alpine, Ryo Hirakawa takes Oliver Bearman's seat at Haas, and Colton Herta fills in for Valtteri Bottas at Cadillac.

What's Next

The Hungaroring's twisting 4.381-kilometre layout — often compared to a giant go-kart track — makes it one of the least power-sensitive circuits on the calendar, which should reduce the influence of engine deployment issues. Pirelli has brought its softest tire allocation of the season (C3, C4, C5), and high track temperatures are expected to make tire degradation a decisive strategic factor. Free Practice 1 gets underway on Friday at 1:30 pm local time (4:30 am PDT), with the 70-lap race set for Sunday at 3:00 pm local (6:00 am PDT).
nri_angle: The Hungarian GP is the final race before F1's summer break, a pivotal moment in a championship that has captivated global audiences with its dramatic AI-powered regulation era.
